kind: multi_country_combination
status: approved
buttonLabel: "Explore tours through Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay"
lead: >-
  Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay come together in a journey of striking contrasts: Rio de Janeiro, Iguazu Falls, Buenos Aires and the shores of the Río de la Plata. However, how smoothly the itinerary works depends on the order of flights and ferry crossings, re-entry into Argentina, different currencies and the beach season in Punta del Este. We examine current Ada Tours itineraries, travel documents, border crossings and how to divide your time between the three countries.
---

## Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay: choosing a journey through three countries

This combination lets you experience South America's contrasts between nature and cities on a single journey. In [Brazil](/brazil/), you discover [Rio de Janeiro](/brazil/place/rio-de-janeiro/) and the waterfalls on the [Foz do Iguaçu](/brazil/place/foz-do-iguacu/) side. In [Argentina](/argentina/), travelers visit [Buenos Aires](/argentina/place/buenos-aires/) and the [Argentine side of Iguazu](/argentina/place/puerto-iguazu/). In [Uruguay](/uruguay/), the route leads from the colonial streets of [Colonia del Sacramento](/uruguay/place/colonia-del-sacramento/) to [Montevideo](/uruguay/place/montevideo/) and the beaches of [Punta del Este](/uruguay/place/punta-del-este/).

Our catalog contains {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} with all three countries as principal destinations. **That does not mean every tour is limited to exactly three countries:** some add Chile and Patagonia. The decisive considerations are not the number of countries in the headline but the actual order of stops, transfers and excursions.

## Which current itineraries fit?

| Tour | What makes it different |
|---|---|
| [13 days: Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-uruguay-13-days/) | Three countries, Iguazu, cities and time by the ocean |
| [17 days: Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Uruguay](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-chile-uruguay/) | Adds Chilean and Argentine Patagonia |
| [26 days: Argentina and Patagonia](/multi-country/tour/best-of-argentina-patagonia-26-days/) | Extended exploration of Argentina with visits to neighboring countries |

The **[13-day itinerary](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-uruguay-13-days/)** is closest to a classic tour of exactly these three countries. Rio and Iguazu come first, followed by Buenos Aires. On day seven, the route crosses the Río de la Plata by ferry, visits Colonia del Sacramento and continues toward Montevideo. Punta del Este follows, and the journey ends with a return to Buenos Aires. Uruguay occupies several days, not just a short excursion to the opposite shore.

The **[17-day journey](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-chile-uruguay/)** begins in Chile, takes in Torres del Paine and Perito Moreno Glacier, then continues through Buenos Aires, Uruguay, both sides of Iguazu, Rio and Búzios. It requires a wider range of clothing: the beach weather of Brazil is combined with wind and cold in Patagonia. Do not treat it as an extended version of the 13-day trip with the same overnight stops.

The **[26-day Argentina and Patagonia itinerary](/multi-country/tour/best-of-argentina-patagonia-26-days/)** has a different emphasis. It explores Argentina's regions in depth: Buenos Aires, northern valleys, wine regions, lakes and glaciers. The journey includes Montevideo, the Brazilian side of Iguazu and Chile's Torres del Paine, but Argentina itself remains the main subject. If you want to explore Uruguay extensively and spend several days in Punta del Este, compare it with the 13-day tour.

## Which travel sequence works best?

On the 13-day itinerary, the order **Rio → Iguazu → Buenos Aires → Uruguay → Buenos Aires** solves several logistical problems. The waterfalls sit on the Brazil–Argentina border, making it convenient to visit both sides of the natural complex during one segment. After flying to Argentina's capital, you can then reach Uruguay by water without returning to Brazil.

Visiting both sides of Iguazu requires **an actual international border crossing**. [Foz do Iguaçu](/brazil/place/foz-do-iguacu/) and [Puerto Iguazu](/argentina/place/puerto-iguazu/) are in different countries; moving between them is not a simple walk within one park. Allow for documents, immigration procedures, transport to the entrances and potential queues on the excursion day.

The crossing from Buenos Aires to Uruguay is also international. Ferry companies serve Colonia and Montevideo; depending on the ticket, the trip may combine a sea crossing to Colonia with an onward bus. **Crossing time, check-in and passport control are separate elements of the timetable.** Do not assume that the sailing time printed on a ticket is the same as the full journey from hotel checkout to check-in at another city.

Returning from Uruguay to Buenos Aires means **re-entering Argentina**. Travelers whose nationality requires a visa must check whether repeat entry is allowed and what kind of authorization is needed. Passport control is repeated even when visa-free travel applies. If you have an onward international flight, allow additional time between the ferry arrival and airport departure.

## Visas and documents: three separate entry regimes

As of **October 15, 2026**, official lists for Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay state that Russian citizens with ordinary passports may visit these countries for tourism without obtaining a tourist visa in advance, within the limits of the respective agreements. **This rule applies specifically to Russian nationality and tourist entry.** Different requirements may apply to other passports, employment, extended stays or connections outside these three countries.

A visa and permission to enter are not the same thing. At each border, officials may check passport validity, the purpose and duration of travel, evidence of departure, accommodation and available funds. When planning the itinerary, we help identify the necessary crossings and documentation checks for the traveler's nationality. Border authorities make the final admission decision.

On the 13-day tour, it is especially important to list **the second entry into Argentina after Uruguay** separately. On the 17- and 26-day tours, Chile's rules must also be considered because Chile is part of those routes. Booking tickets with minimal time for several independent checks creates unnecessary risk.

## Currencies, cash and bank cards

Each country has its own currency:

| Country | Currency |
|---|---|
| [Brazil](/brazil/) | Brazilian real, BRL |
| [Argentina](/argentina/) | Argentine peso, ARS |
| [Uruguay](/uruguay/) | Uruguayan peso, UYU |

US dollars may be useful for exchange or particular tourist expenses, but **they cannot replace local currency for all everyday purchases**. In Argentina, check the applicable rules and actual exchange conditions close to the travel date instead of relying on outdated stories about exchange rates. Plan for local currency in Uruguay's cities and resorts too.

If your card was issued by a Russian bank, you cannot judge its ability to work abroad simply by the payment-system logo. Acceptance depends on the issuer, the international network currently available and the individual terminal. Even a card issued by a foreign bank carries no universal guarantee. Before departure, check its operation in each of the three countries, cash-withdrawal fees, limits and a backup payment option. We can help plan the route's currency needs, but **Ada Tours is not a currency-exchange office and cannot guarantee that any particular card will work**.

The budget goes beyond the tour price. Independent expenses may include meals not already paid for, local transport during free time, entrance tickets outside the itinerary, communications and personal purchases. Each offer specifies its own terms; a budget calculated for one program should not be applied automatically to another.

## Weather and clothing: Rio, Iguazu and Uruguay's coast

In the Southern Hemisphere, summer runs from December to February. But **Rio's summer weather differs from conditions on Uruguay's Atlantic coast**. Rio is often hot and humid, Iguazu can be hot with heavy downpours, while the exposed beaches of Punta del Este may be windy even in summer.

| Stage | What to pack |
|---|---|
| Rio and Iguazu | Light clothes, sun and rain protection |
| Buenos Aires | Comfortable shoes and an extra layer |
| Punta del Este | Beachwear and a windbreaker |
| Patagonia, if included | Warm clothing and wind protection |

**December through March** is particularly relevant for Uruguay's beach season, but the country remains interesting in other months: Colonia and Montevideo are cultural destinations all year. For Iguazu, use the actual forecast, precipitation and temperatures on your dates rather than a blanket statement about “good weather all year round.”

The climatic contrast is much greater on the 17- and 26-day itineraries including Patagonia. Thermal base layers and a wind-resistant jacket are more useful there than another set of beach clothes. Check airline baggage allowances for each domestic segment; different carriers may have different rules.

## Health, insurance and spare time

For national parks and tropical regions, discuss prevention of mosquito-borne illness with your doctor in advance. Brazil's Ministry of Health recommends yellow fever vaccination for travel to certain risk areas; vaccination is generally planned at least **10 days** before visiting such a region. A health recommendation and a mandatory vaccination certificate for a specific border are different matters. Check up-to-date medical information and individual contraindications for routes through Rio and Iguazu.

Travel insurance needs to match your activities and destinations. An ordinary city tour, a boat excursion near Iguazu and walking on glacier trails in Patagonia can require different kinds of cover. Travelers with chronic conditions or limited mobility should discuss stairs, humidity, heat and walking distances beforehand.

A practical principle for all three countries is to **allow extra time at international connections and avoid scheduling important events immediately after a border crossing**. A delayed ferry or flight affects subsequent accommodation and excursions. We help plan the sequence, coordinate road transfers and build in reasonable buffers based on confirmed schedules.

## Frequently asked questions

### How much time should I allow for three countries?

For a route covering Rio, both sides of Iguazu, Buenos Aires and several Uruguayan cities, there is a ready-made [13-day itinerary](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-uruguay-13-days/). Longer 17- and 26-day options suit travelers who want to include Chile and Patagonia, but the nature of the journey will be different.

### Do Russians need one shared visa for Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay?

There is no common visa for all three countries. Under official lists checked on October 15, 2026, Russian citizens can make short tourist visits to each without obtaining a visa in advance, subject to the respective rules. Other nationalities and purposes of entry require separate checks. Each border crossing is still a distinct procedure.

### Can I see both sides of Iguazu Falls on one trip?

Yes. The [13-day tour](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-uruguay-13-days/) includes the Brazilian Iguazu leg and an excursion on the Argentine side. Allow time to cross the border and observe actual opening hours.

### How do I get from Buenos Aires to Uruguay?

A principal option is the ferry across the Río de la Plata. You can sail to [Colonia del Sacramento](/uruguay/place/colonia-del-sacramento/) and travel overland to [Montevideo](/uruguay/place/montevideo/), or select other services offered by ferry companies. The exact departure depends on the tour dates, and passport control is mandatory.

### Should I add Patagonia?

If glaciers and mountains are your priority, look at the [17-day four-country itinerary](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-chile-uruguay/) and the [26-day program](/multi-country/tour/best-of-argentina-patagonia-26-days/). Both require more time, different luggage and extra flights. For a classic urban and beach journey, comparing the three countries without the southern regions is sufficient.

On the 26-day tour, most trekking and off-road travel takes place in Patagonia, while the most substantial 4x4 section of the 20- and 32-day itineraries is in Bolivia. ## Which adventures actually feature in this three-country combination?

Our collection contains {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} with [Argentina](/argentina/), [Brazil](/brazil/) and [Uruguay](/uruguay/) among the principal destinations. However, **the itineraries do not stop at these three countries**. Some continue along the Andes into Chile and Bolivia; others reach Peru, Ecuador and Colombia.

There is an important distinction here: the adventure theme applies to the tour as a whole. It may refer to independent trekking in Argentina, an off-road journey in Patagonia or a high-altitude 4x4 route **in Bolivia**, outside the three selected countries. Before choosing, ask where the active days actually take place, how much time is allocated to them and which activities are already included.

For alternatives, explore [multi-country adventure journeys](/multi-country/interests/adventure/) or the [adventure tour section](/interests/adventure/).

## Argentina: Patagonia as the main active leg

The clearest match among these three-country combinations is the [26-day tour of Argentina and Patagonia](/multi-country/tour/best-of-argentina-patagonia-26-days/). It connects Buenos Aires, Iguazu, northern regions, lakes, glaciers and Tierra del Fuego.

Around [El Chaltén](/argentina/place/el-chalten/), the itinerary leaves days free for independent hikes on mountain trails. Kayaking is available as an optional extra on one day. **A free trekking day means choosing a route according to your experience and the weather, not an automatically included guided excursion.** At [El Calafate](/argentina/place/el-calafate/), the visit to Perito Moreno Glacier is a different experience from an independent mountain hike.

Further south, Ushuaia includes a group 4x4 outing to the lakes. This is a different kind of activity: most of the journey takes place in a vehicle rather than on a full walking trek. Separate hiking demands, driving segments and optional activities when planning.

This Argentine itinerary particularly suits travelers who want several days in Patagonia rather than a short sightseeing stop. Compare it with less extensive routes through the [Argentina tours catalog](/argentina/tour/).

## Brazil: Iguazu Falls and nature excursions

The waterfall region is prominent on all three options. The Brazilian side of Iguazu reveals the broad front of the cascades, while on the [Argentine side near Puerto Iguazu](/argentina/place/puerto-iguazu/), the excursion follows a system of walkways and viewing platforms. This is a walking-based nature experience, but it should not be presented as demanding trekking.

The longer 20- and 32-day journeys include a possible Macuco Safari excursion around Iguazu, with a forest segment and a boat ride. Check the conditions and price of this activity for the specific day: **the fact that an excursion is offered alongside the main itinerary does not establish that it is included**.

[Rio de Janeiro](/brazil/place/rio-de-janeiro/) combines the ocean, mountain views and city sightseeing. Going up Corcovado or Sugarloaf Mountain does not become a sporting hike just because the landscape is dramatic. Travelers looking for genuine physical activity should check for a separately confirmed walk or excursion rather than choose a tour based on photographs of peaks.

## Uruguay: a cultural pause between active stages

All three itineraries visit [Montevideo](/uruguay/place/montevideo/). On the 20- and 32-day programs, this is arranged as a full-day outing from Buenos Aires: a ferry across the Río de la Plata, sightseeing in the capital and then a return journey. The 26-day tour also features the city as a day excursion.

There is no confirmed rafting, mountain ascent or multi-day trekking here. Montevideo is **an urban and cultural stop** offering a change of pace between busy travel segments. Seeking a sporting program here merely because the complete tour is marked as adventurous would be misleading.

Allow enough time for the ferry, formalities and return to Argentina without conflicting with the next flight. Your chosen itinerary determines where this stop falls in the journey.

## Three available itineraries: choosing between them

{{catalog.tourTable:tour_latin_america_six_countries_20_days_2026,tour_south_america_eight_countries_32_days_2026,tour_source_vsya_argentina}}

The [26-day Patagonia itinerary](/multi-country/tour/best-of-argentina-patagonia-26-days/) suits travelers interested in Argentina's mountain trails and independent hikes. Its active days are closely tied to Argentina, including a 4x4 outing in Ushuaia. One important consideration is which hikes are independent and whether you want to arrange a guide in advance.

The [20-day tour through six countries](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-6-countries-20-days/) crosses more borders, continuing after Uruguay via Chile to the highlands of Bolivia. The 4x4 vehicles and Uyuni Salt Flat belong to the Bolivian segment, so this three-country collection title does not identify where the main off-road experience takes place.

The [32-day eight-country journey](/multi-country/tour/south-america-eight-countries-32-days/) extends the same pattern into Ecuador and Colombia. Besides the high-altitude route, it includes the Galápagos Islands and various nature excursions. The longer itinerary covers more regions but increases the number of flights, hotel changes and different climates.

Choosing between them depends on what you value more: **several days hiking in Patagonia** or **an extensive journey with adventure stages in neighboring countries**.

## What to arrange before departure

In Patagonia, weather can change during the day. Choose an independent trail according to the actual forecast, its length and your abilities. For off-road excursions, check driving times, stops and road surfaces. At Iguazu, waterproof protection for equipment and comfortable non-slip footwear are helpful.

These longer itineraries combine tropical Brazil, the temperate climate of Buenos Aires and cool mountain regions in southern Argentina. If the journey continues to Bolivia, high altitude and different overnight conditions add further requirements. Pack for the actual stages of your trip rather than the weather in the first city.

Ada Tours helps coordinate cross-border transport and distinguish included excursions from optional experiences. For self-guided trekking, it is particularly important to establish who is responsible for navigation, whether a guide is needed and what alternative is available if the weather is poor. Border and insurance rules depend on nationality and travel dates: a ready-made itinerary does not mean universal conditions for all travelers.

## Frequently asked questions about adventures in Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay

### Is there trekking in all three countries?

No. Confirmed independent trekking days are primarily in Argentina's El Chaltén area on the 26-day itinerary. Uruguay features a city tour of Montevideo.

### Is every tour in this selection suited to mountain hiking?

No. On the 20- and 32-day itineraries, adventure is significantly associated with the off-road section in Bolivia. For several days of trekking in Argentina, examine the [Patagonia itinerary](/multi-country/tour/best-of-argentina-patagonia-26-days/).

### Can I see both sides of Iguazu?

Yes. The itineraries considered include visits to Iguazu Falls from the Brazilian and Argentine sides. Check the specific day's excursion route, time for the border and possible optional activities.

### Is kayaking near El Chaltén included in the tour price?

On the 26-day itinerary, it is an optional paid activity. The basic package should not be assumed to include kayaking unless this option is confirmed.

### Which option is better with limited time?

If seeing several countries in one journey matters most, compare the [20-day itinerary](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-6-countries-20-days/) with your tolerance for frequent transfers. If Patagonia and hiking are your priorities, allocating sufficient time to southern Argentina matters more, even if that means dropping other countries.

buttonLabel: "Explore the cultures of Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay"
lead: >-
  Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay make a rewarding cultural route through cities and the shores of the Río de la Plata: historic Rio, the neighborhoods of Buenos Aires, gaucho traditions, and the architecture of Colonia del Sacramento and Montevideo. However, the depth of the Uruguayan segment varies considerably: one tour includes several nights, while others make only a brief visit.
---

## What connects these three countries culturally?

Our themed collection contains {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} traveling through Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay. Its interest extends beyond the geographic proximity of Argentina and Uruguay. Travelers compare Rio's Portuguese heritage, Buenos Aires' urban culture, and two historical influences on the shores of the Río de la Plata: Spanish and Portuguese.

The most important decision is **how much time to devote to Uruguay**. The [13-day Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay tour](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-uruguay-13-days/) visits Colonia del Sacramento, Montevideo and Punta del Este in sequence. On the [four-country itinerary with Chile](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-chile-uruguay/), Uruguay is represented by a one-day trip to Montevideo. The [26-day Argentina and Patagonia journey](/multi-country/tour/best-of-argentina-patagonia-26-days/) also includes an excursion to Uruguay, but most of the time is spent in Argentina.

In other words, selecting three countries in the filter does not mean experiencing each culture in equal depth. The [general Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay collection](/multi-country/argentina_brazil_uruguay/) helps compare geography; here the main question is **which cities and traditions you will actually discover**.

## Brazil: Rio as a cultural landscape

In [Rio de Janeiro](/brazil/place/rio-de-janeiro/), travelers ascend to Corcovado and Sugarloaf Mountain and explore the historic center. The city lies between hills, the ocean and Guanabara Bay. That setting has shaped both its architecture and neighborhood life. Rio's cultural landscape is recognized by UNESCO.

The 13-day itinerary includes the cathedral, Sambadrome, theater, National Library and other buildings on a general city tour. Viewing these landmarks introduces the city's history and architecture, but **Carnival tickets are not part of an ordinary sightseeing itinerary**. The mention of the Sambadrome does not imply that an event ticket is included.

After Rio, the journey continues to [Foz do Iguaçu](/brazil/place/foz-do-iguacu/) and, on some programs, the Argentine side of the waterfalls. This is a major nature stop rather than a separate cultural excursion. If Brazilian history is your principal interest, consider [cultural tours in Brazil](/interests/culture-and-history/tours/brazil/).

## Argentina: Buenos Aires and gaucho culture

In [Buenos Aires](/argentina/place/buenos-aires/), travelers visit Plaza de Mayo, Casa Rosada, old La Boca, San Telmo and other neighborhoods. Compared with Rio, the urban culture of the Río de la Plata is particularly evident here in the architecture, public spaces and traditions of a capital connected to a vast river estuary.

The 13-day itinerary includes a separate visit to the Don Silvano ranch to discover gaucho life and the folklore of the pampas. This is an important contrast with an ordinary city tour: traditions are experienced outside the metropolitan center. The four-country journey also includes a ranch day and gaucho festivities, while the evening program features a tango show.

**Tango is known throughout the Río de la Plata region, but its actual inclusion must be checked against each itinerary.** A confirmed ranch visit and city tour do not mean a tango-show ticket has already been paid for. For other combinations, see [cultural and historical tours in Argentina](/interests/culture-and-history/tours/argentina/).

## Uruguay: two very different ways to visit

On the [13-day three-country itinerary](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-uruguay-13-days/), travelers cross the Río de la Plata by ferry from Buenos Aires to [Colonia del Sacramento](/uruguay/place/colonia-del-sacramento/). The city's historic quarter developed through both Portuguese and Spanish influences and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its small streets, older houses and street layout tell a very different story from the broad avenues of Buenos Aires.

The route then continues to [Montevideo](/uruguay/place/montevideo/) for a city tour including Independence Square, Constitution Square and the historic center. After the city visits, it heads toward [Punta del Este](/uruguay/place/punta-del-este/), with several days allocated to the beach. The format changes here: Punta del Este should not be presented as a continuation of an intensive museum program.

On the [Brazil–Argentina–Chile–Uruguay four-country tour](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-chile-uruguay/), Montevideo is a short independent excursion from Buenos Aires, not several days including Colonia and the coast. On the 26-day Argentina itinerary, the Montevideo visit is likewise an additional cross-border cultural experience within a long Patagonian route.

**Choose according to the time actually spent in Uruguay:** a single sightseeing day and a four-day stay with overnight stops provide very different experiences of the country.

## Choosing between 13, 17 and 26 days

**13 days:** a logical cultural progression from Rio to Buenos Aires, Colonia and Montevideo, ending with beach time in Punta del Este. This is best if you want to see Uruguay's historic town and spend several days in the country. The route also includes Iguazu Falls and an Argentine ranch.

**17 days:** the [four-country itinerary](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-chile-uruguay/) begins in Chile, visits Patagonia and Argentina, makes a brief excursion to Uruguay, and continues into Brazil. Cultural stops are interspersed with longer nature stages; the variety of experiences is broader.

**26 days:** the [extended Argentina and Patagonia tour](/multi-country/tour/best-of-argentina-patagonia-26-days/) covers Argentina's wine and mountain regions, Patagonia, Iguazu Falls and separate trips to neighboring countries. If your goal is the history of all three nations, the longer duration does not, by itself, mean more time in Uruguay.

These durations refer to the named itineraries. Check the precise length and content of any other available tour in its own description.

## Ferries, borders and the pace of cultural travel

The ferry across the Río de la Plata is a significant part of the journey when it appears in the itinerary. Before departure, confirm the port, check-in time, border-crossing document, luggage rules and the connection with onward sightseeing. Ferry timetables and rules for different passports may change, so they cannot be fixed without specific travel dates.

A busy city day in Rio or Buenos Aires can easily become overloaded with additional museums. Uruguay offers a less intense pace, but travelers may want time to walk through historic Colonia. We help coordinate the sequence, arrange transport, allocate overnight stays and distinguish included excursions from optional additions.

## Frequently asked questions about the cultures of Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay

### Which itinerary includes Colonia del Sacramento?

A visit to [Colonia del Sacramento](/uruguay/place/colonia-del-sacramento/) is confirmed on the [13-day three-country itinerary](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-uruguay-13-days/). On the other options discussed, Uruguay is represented mainly by Montevideo, so do not assume Colonia is included.

### Is a tango show included on every three-country tour?

No, inclusion depends on the exact itinerary. For example, the [17-day four-country journey](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-chile-uruguay/) lists a tango show, while an important cultural day on the 13-day tour focuses on a gaucho ranch.

### Do I need a separate visa for the ferry between Argentina and Uruguay?

Check entry and exit rules for your nationality and travel dates: the ferry crosses an international border. Holding a ferry ticket does not replace the required entry documents.

### Should I spend more time in Montevideo or Buenos Aires?

Buenos Aires offers more for exploring extensive urban neighborhoods, tango and pampas culture. Montevideo is well suited to Río de la Plata architecture and relaxed walks. For Portuguese and Spanish heritage, consider adding Colonia del Sacramento and selecting an itinerary with enough time in Uruguay.

lead: >-
  What makes journeys through Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay interesting for food lovers depends on the specific itinerary. On the 26-day tour, the wine experience is concentrated in Argentina: wineries in Cafayate, Luján de Cuyo and the Uco Valley, with visits and tastings. Uruguay introduces local food during a one-day visit to Montevideo, while the Brazilian leg focuses on Iguazu. ## Food and wine in three countries: where real tastings are included

Here you will find {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} featuring Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay among their principal destinations. Both are categorized under “Food and wine,” but **that is not a promise of three wine regions in each country**. Look at which wineries, markets, dinners and excursions actually appear on the itinerary.

[Argentina](/argentina/) offers the most substantial wine program. The [26-day Argentina and Patagonia journey](/multi-country/tour/best-of-argentina-patagonia-26-days/) includes a winery visit in [Cafayate](/argentina/place/cafayate/), followed by separate excursion days around [Mendoza](/argentina/place/mendoza/): three wineries in [Luján de Cuyo](/argentina/place/lujan-de-cuyo/) and two in the [Uco Valley](/argentina/place/uco-valley/). You explore winemaking and take part in tastings, while the Luján de Cuyo and Uco Valley days include lunches with views of the Andes.

In [Uruguay](/uruguay/), that same itinerary visits [Montevideo](/uruguay/place/montevideo/) for one day from Buenos Aires. The city tour includes a market where you can explore local produce and cuisine. This is a food-related experience, but **no mandatory winery visit in Uruguay is confirmed**.

In [Brazil](/brazil/), both itineraries under discussion focus on [Foz do Iguaçu](/brazil/place/foz-do-iguacu/) and the waterfalls. A food-and-wine label does not by itself confirm a Brazilian winery, cooking class or tasting restaurant. If you would like a dedicated culinary day, discuss that option with us when adapting the program.

## Two itineraries, two different culinary experiences

**The 26-day itinerary** introduces Argentine winemaking across several regions. First comes the northwest and Cafayate, with vineyards, a winery and a wine museum. Then Mendoza, where visits to Luján de Cuyo and the Uco Valley take place on separate days. This allows time to compare the regions and production methods instead of making a single stop at a wine shop.

**The 20-day journey through six Latin American countries** is organized differently. In [Buenos Aires](/argentina/place/buenos-aires/), a tango show with dinner is planned; the excursion description mentions Argentine wines. Montevideo is dedicated to the historic center and sightseeing, while Brazil includes Rio de Janeiro and Iguazu. A winery visit to the Maipo Valley in Chile is available **as an optional excursion for an additional fee**. ## Cafayate, Luján de Cuyo and Uco: why separate wine days matter

[Cafayate](/argentina/place/cafayate/) is in northwestern Argentina, reached on this tour after flying to Salta. The itinerary includes visiting a winery, learning about grape cultivation and production methods, a wine museum and an overnight stay at a wine hotel. It combines discovering a wine-growing region with travel through Salta's mountainous landscape.

[Luján de Cuyo](/argentina/place/lujan-de-cuyo/) offers a different experience. The program includes three wineries, tastings, an introduction to production and lunch at the third winery. The region is widely known for Malbec. It is about more than tasting wine: the excursion shows how vineyards at the foot of the Andes are shaped by local climate and agricultural traditions.

The [Uco Valley](/argentina/place/uco-valley/) has its own day with two wineries and lunch. That lets you compare vineyards and tastings with the previous day without a long transfer into another country. Different producers may use different grapes and winemaking methods; the exact brands and labels must be confirmed against the scheduled visits rather than invented in advance.

For other journeys focused on this specialty, explore [food and wine tours in Argentina](/interests/food-and-wine/tours/argentina/). They may be more convenient if you want to concentrate on wineries and reduce the nature-related transfers of the extended itinerary.

## A one-day culinary stop in Montevideo

[Montevideo](/uruguay/place/montevideo/) is visited by ferry from Buenos Aires. The 26-day tour includes ferry tickets, an English-language sightseeing excursion and a visit to a city market. Travelers return to Argentina the same day.

For food lovers this is a useful stop, but it leaves less time for extended tastings than an overnight stay in Uruguay. It would be misleading to promise city sightseeing, several restaurants, a winery outside the capital and a relaxed return on the evening ferry unless that sequence is actually scheduled.

Before traveling, check opening hours of the market or restaurant you want to visit, food-allergy arrangements and the buffer before the return ferry. We can discuss changing stops or spending longer in Uruguay, but additional visits and their prices must be agreed separately.

## Why Iguazu remains a nature stop on a food-themed itinerary

The Brazilian and Argentine sides of Iguazu provide a dramatic natural contrast to Mendoza's wineries. The program includes visiting the waterfalls and walking in national parks. This is an important part of the journey, even if the client's principal interest is regional cuisine and wine.

Inventing a Brazilian culinary tour here would be wrong. If a traveler wants a particular regional dish, restaurant or workshop, that calls for separate planning: the city, available hours, menu, transport and confirmed price must all be established. [General tours in Brazil](/brazil/tour/) provide other routes through the country, but should not automatically be classified as culinary programs.

## Nature in Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay: what these itineraries share

**Iguazu Falls on the border between Brazil and Argentina is the main natural attraction shared by this collection.** Beyond that, the routes diverge sharply: the shorter three-country journey includes Uruguay's coast, while longer itineraries may add glaciers in Chile and Argentina or the high-altitude landscapes of Bolivia and Peru.

Our collection contains {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} featuring Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay as principal countries with nature experiences on the itinerary. **Some routes visit more than three countries.** The same filter does not imply identical stops or the same amount of time at each attraction.

Travel documents, ferries and border procedures are covered in the [Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay travel collection](/multi-country/argentina_brazil_uruguay/). Here, the focus is different: which trips feature the waterfalls and coastline, and which have their principal nature experiences in additional countries along the route.

## Iguazu: forest and cascades on both sides of the border

On the Brazilian side, [Foz do Iguaçu](/brazil/place/foz-do-iguacu/) offers wide panoramic views of the cascades. On the Argentine side, [Puerto Iguazu](/argentina/place/puerto-iguazu/) has different walking routes and opportunities to approach individual waterfall sections. Seeing both gives a more complete picture of the natural complex, but takes additional time and requires crossing an international border.

The [13-day tour through three countries](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-uruguay-13-days/) includes stops around Iguazu, with an Argentine-side excursion. The [17-day four-country itinerary](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-chile-uruguay/) also visits the cascades from different sides. Check the actual excursions day by day: the word “Iguazu” in a route description does not confirm both national parks.

Walkways near the falls may be wet from spray, and the climate differs from the cooler south. The park protects subtropical forests, but **simply being there does not promise sightings of rare animals**. If you want a dedicated safari, choose a tour with that specific activity rather than only the [Nature](/interests/nature/) theme.

## Uruguay: ocean and coastal walks, or just one day in the capital

On the [13-day journey](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-uruguay-13-days/), the route continues after Argentina and the waterfalls through [Colonia del Sacramento](/uruguay/place/colonia-del-sacramento/), [Montevideo](/uruguay/place/montevideo/) and [Punta del Este](/uruguay/place/punta-del-este/). Several days at the resort allow time for walks by the sea and coastal relaxation. This is a separate part of the journey, but it is not an expedition through Uruguay's protected natural areas.

On the [17-day four-country journey](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-chile-uruguay/), by contrast, Uruguay is represented by a visit to Montevideo. The [26-day Argentina and Patagonia program](/multi-country/tour/best-of-argentina-patagonia-26-days/) likewise includes a day trip to Uruguay's capital from Buenos Aires, returning afterward. The city's Rambla follows the waterfront and offers coastal views, but such a visit **is not several nights of a beach vacation**.

Choose according to your aim. If the ocean and free time matter, check the actual overnight stays in Punta del Este. If you want a brief change of country between nature excursions, a day in Montevideo is more suitable. Do not promise whales or Uruguay's national parks unless those visits are part of the specific itinerary.

## Who needs Patagonia, and who will prefer Iguazu and the ocean?

Some itineraries continue through Chile and Argentine Patagonia. The 17-day tour includes [Torres del Paine](/chile/place/puerto-natales-torres-del-paine/), then [El Calafate](/argentina/place/el-calafate/) and [Perito Moreno Glacier](/argentina/place/perito-moreno-glacier/). Travelers later reach Iguazu Falls and the Brazilian coast. This lets you compare glaciers, subtropical forest and ocean within one trip.

On the [26-day itinerary](/multi-country/tour/best-of-argentina-patagonia-26-days/), much more time is dedicated to Argentina's natural landscapes: [Bariloche](/argentina/place/bariloche/) with lakes and forests, El Calafate, El Chaltén, Ushuaia and an excursion to Chile's Torres del Paine. In this context, Uruguay remains a brief sightseeing stop rather than a separate nature-focused destination.

There is also a different alternative: the [20-day tour through six countries](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-6-countries-20-days/) continues via Santiago and Atacama to Bolivia and Peru. **It does not become a Patagonia tour simply because Argentina and Chile are on its route.** If Perito Moreno is your priority, select an itinerary explicitly including the glacier.

First check how many days are allocated to Iguazu. Next determine whether the trip offers beach time in Punta del Este or only a sightseeing visit to Montevideo. Only then compare additional nature regions, principally Patagonia or the Andes. This prevents a longer itinerary from appearing more nature-focused merely because it lists more countries, even though your preferred attraction receives just one day.

Every format involves seasonal compromises. Beach dates are particularly important for Punta del Este; at Iguazu, consider humidity and walkway conditions; Patagonia requires warm clothes and protection against wind. **There is no single ideal weather pattern for all the natural stops.** Translate the preliminary climate information into practical needs for footwear, clothing and spare time.

## Borders and logistics: where time is lost

Visiting Iguazu from both sides requires crossing from Brazil to Argentina. Reaching Uruguay requires a ferry or other transport from the [Buenos Aires](/argentina/place/buenos-aires/) area. Additional countries mean more flights and potential border crossings. If you return to Argentina after Uruguay or Chile, your documents must permit re-entry under the rules applicable to your nationality.

Ada Tours helps coordinate travel order and the actual days available for rest. However, additional excursions, hotel nights or private transport cannot be treated as automatically included: each itinerary defines its own services. When selecting a nature tour, it is more useful to protect time at the attraction you most want to visit than to squeeze in another city.

## Frequently asked questions about nature in Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay

### Does every tour in this collection include Patagonia?

No. Patagonia appears only on some itineraries with additional destinations in Chile. To visit glaciers, look for a specific day in El Calafate and at Perito Moreno, not merely the word “Argentina.”

### Can I combine the waterfalls with a beach stay in Uruguay?

Yes. The [13-day itinerary](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-uruguay-13-days/) includes stops in Punta del Este. Check the daily program for the amount of free time and accommodation.

### Can I watch wildlife in Uruguay during a short visit to Montevideo?

A city sightseeing day cannot be described as a dedicated wildlife-watching excursion. The Rambla and coastal views are a different experience from a specialist animal-watching trip.
